svg.aria-label: Top: textbook RRF rewards items that appear in both lists, while in Strobe the image and text keys never overlap so RRF reduces to alternating image and text hits. Bottom: the real eval question 'skyscrapers in the city on a cloudy day' where the fused list pushes the expected photo from rank 2 to rank 3.
svg.title: RRF in Strobe is an interleave
svg.text: What RRF actually does in Strobe: a round-robin interleave
Image hits are keyed by S3 object key, text hits by post#id or comment#id. No item can appear in both lists, so no score is ever summed.
A · Textbook RRF: lists share items
e.g. keyword search + vector search over the same documents
d2 was only 2nd in list A, but both retrievers agreed on it, so it wins by a wide margin.
This is what RRF is for: agreement across systems is evidence of relevance.
Here k matters: it sets how much a single top rank is worth against agreement lower down.
B · Strobe: the lists never share an item
image key u/p/f · text key post#p or comment#c
Every score has one term, so ties come in pairs. Python's stable sort keeps insertion
order, and the image list is gathered first: image, text, image, text …
Any k > 0 gives this same order. k = 60 changes nothing here.
C · A REAL QUESTION FROM THE EVAL
"skyscrapers in the city on a cloudy day"
no expected_post_ids → nothing can score → RR = 0
The fused list is not worse at finding the photo: it put the photo's own post at rank 2. The scoring only credits imageId 74539674, and the image index's #1 is
a second upload of the same city.jpeg (re-seeded from _originals/ on 25 Sep) that the labels don't know about. The same pattern explains all four questions where fused lost MRR.
* The two George Street posts have identical text, so their vectors tie and their order can swap between runs.
